Positioning plan for the [selected build](bom.qmd#selected-build): up to 4
subwoofers and 6 perimeter error microphones in the real bedroom,
$L_x \times L_y \times L_z = 4.445 \times 3.658 \times 2.692\ \mathrm{m}$
($14'7'' \times 12'0''$, ceiling $8'10''$). Furniture: bed (head at a wall)
and a double dresser (~$1.5 \times 0.5\ \mathrm{m}$, 0.9 m tall); no desk.
Coordinates below put the origin at the corner marked S1, $x$ along the
14′7″ wall, $z$ up.

![Top view and elevation. Generated by
[`scripts/room_layout.py`](https://github.com/madi-lts/roomANC/blob/claude/determined-ritchie-ma10cm/scripts/room_layout.py).](images/room-layout.png){#fig-layout}

## The room's modes vs. the measured tones

Rigid-wall eigenfrequencies
$f_{n_x n_y n_z} = \frac{c}{2}\sqrt{(n_x/L_x)^2 + (n_y/L_y)^2 + (n_z/L_z)^2}$
for the lowest families, against the [measured tone census](measurements.qmd):

| Mode | $f$ (Hz) | Nearby measured line |
|---|---:|---|
| (1,0,0) | 38.6 | **39.9 Hz** machine #2 fundamental |
| (0,1,0) | 46.9 | — |
| **(1,1,0)** | **60.7** | **59.0 Hz** drone fundamental |
| **(0,0,1)** | **63.7** | 59.0 Hz (second near-resonance) |
| (2,0,0) | 77.2 | 79.9 Hz (2 × 39.9) |
| (0,1,1) | 79.1 | 79.9 Hz |
| (3,0,0) | 115.7 | 117.9 Hz (2 × 59.0) |
| (1,2,1) | 119.8 | 120.0 Hz mains hum |
| (2,2,0) | 121.4 | 120.0 Hz |

With $T_{60} \approx 0.4$ s the modal half-power bandwidth is
$\Delta f = 2.2/T_{60} \approx 5.5\ \mathrm{Hz}$, so the 59.0 Hz drone sits
inside the resonance band of **(1,1,0)** and at the edge of **(0,0,1)**, and
the 39.9 Hz machine rides **(1,0,0)**. The room is resonantly amplifying
both sources — unlucky dimensions, but good news for control: a handful of
identified modes dominate, which is exactly the situation the modal-control
argument assumes. (Rigid-wall values run a few Hz high of reality —
compliant walls lower them — so the coincidences are if anything closer;
the [modal model](modes.qmd) of workstream 2 and the level-vs-position map
will pin them down.)

## Subwoofers: start with 2 (diagonal), expand to 4

Corners are pressure antinodes of every mode, so corner loading remains the
rule. The build starts with the **diagonal pair S1 + S4** and keeps the
other two corners (dashed in the figure) as a drop-in expansion:

- A corner source couples to each mode with sign
  $(\pm 1)^{n_x}(\pm 1)^{n_y}$ by corner. For the diagonal pair the
  **common-mode** drive (both subs in phase) couples to **(1,1,0)** — the
  resonant mode under the 59.0 Hz tone — and to (0,0,1), while the
  **differential** drive couples to (1,0,0) and (0,1,0), though only in a
  fixed combination. Two subs therefore span two independent control
  degrees of freedom per frequency, enough to null the two near-resonant
  modes that dominate at 59 Hz.
- The expansion criterion is empirical (spec R2's grid test): if the
  converged residual at any tone retains a spatial pattern the pair cannot
  null — the signature being error mics converged low while grid points
  between them stay high — add S2 + S3 for four independent corner drives.
  No re-cabling: the interface has the outputs, and the TRS runs are
  ordered at full length from day one.
- Each cabinet pushed into its corner, driver facing the corner (a point
  monopole at $\lambda \approx 5.8\ \mathrm{m}$ — and it hides the exposed
  cone from the cat), crossover at maximum, polarity 0°, isolation pads
  underneath, settings taped and never touched after secondary-path ID
  (spec R7).

## The feedback question

"Feedback from the woofers into the error mics" covers three physically
distinct phenomena; only one of them constrains the geometry.

**1. Reference contamination (the classic ANC feedback instability).**
In a feedforward system with a physical reference microphone, the control
loudspeakers' output leaks back into the reference sensor, closing an
unintended loop — the acoustic analogue of PA howlround, conventionally
fought with feedback-neutralization filters. **This loop does not exist in
our design**: the reference is synthesized inside the controller (a tracked
quadrature oscillator, see the
[spec](spec.qmd#tonal-structure-adaptive-notch-form)), so there is no
acoustic input for the woofers to contaminate. This is the strongest of the
several reasons the synthesized reference was chosen. (If the optional wall
accelerometer is ever used, the woofers couple to the wall and the issue
returns in structure-borne form — it would need a neutralization filter
$\hat{F}(z)$ subtracting the predicted woofer contribution from the sensor.)

**2. Error mics hearing the woofers — not a bug.** The path from each
woofer $l$ to each error mic $m$ *is* the secondary path $S_{ml}(z)$ that
FxLMS is built around; the error mics are supposed to hear the woofers,
because $e_m = d_m + \sum_l s_{ml} * y_l$ is the quantity being driven to
zero. The genuine pathology is **near-field bias**: within the reactive
(evanescent) near field of a source, $kr \lesssim 1$ — i.e.
$r \lesssim \lambda/2\pi \approx 0.93\ \mathrm{m}$ at 59 Hz, where
$k = 2\pi/\lambda$ is the wavenumber and $r$ the source–mic distance — the
pressure is dominated by the local $1/r$-divergent term rather than the
modal field. A mic parked there over-weights its nearest woofer, the
controller "wins" by nulling that one mic locally while under-cancelling
the room, and the $M \times L$ secondary-path matrix picks up one dominant
entry per row and conditions badly. **Rule: every error mic stays at least
1 m from every woofer corner** (including the not-yet-installed phase-2
corners, so the expansion needs no mic moves) — the dashed exclusion arcs
in the figure. The exclusion zone belongs to the *sources*, not the walls:
a rigid wall is a pressure **antinode** ($v_n = 0 \Rightarrow |p|$
maximal in the normal coordinate), so a pressure mic near a wall sits
outside every evanescent zone while reading the modal field at full
strength. The table below satisfies the rule with margin (minimum
1.02 m, M4–S3).

**3. Instability through secondary-path error.** FxLMS remains stable while
the phase of $\hat{S}_{ml}$ is within ±90° of the true path at the control
frequencies. Moving a mic, rotating it, bumping a sub, or large furniture
changes rotate that phase — the fix is procedural, not geometric: fixed
mounts, and re-identification after any disturbance (R7), with a small
leakage term in the weight update for robustness.

## Error microphones: a 6-mic perimeter array

The adaptive loop minimizes $\sum_m e_m^2$, so the deep quiet zone forms
around the microphones, weighted by how well they observe the controlled
modes. All six mics live at the room perimeter (0.2–0.4 m off a wall),
where every mode is at a pressure antinode in the wall-normal coordinate —
best SNR, best observability, no stands in the walkable floor, short
baseboard cable runs. Positions (origin at S1's corner):

| Mic | $x$ (m) | $y$ (m) | $h$ (m) | Where |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| M1 | 1.55 | 3.30 | 0.65 | head wall, pillow left (behind headboard) |
| M2 | 2.15 | 3.30 | 0.65 | head wall, pillow right |
| M3 | 4.25 | 1.45 | 1.10 | right wall |
| M4 | 0.20 | 2.30 | 1.75 | left wall, above $H/2$ |
| M5 | 2.60 | 0.30 | 1.20 | bottom wall, standing on the dresser |
| M6 | 2.95 | 3.40 | 2.10 | head wall, tall stand right of bed |

The generating rules:

1. **Boundary placement with two exceptions-by-construction.** Perimeter
   mics null the *controllable* modal field globally — zeroing wall
   pressure zeroes the mode amplitudes. But the *uncontrollable* residual
   (structure-borne direct radiation, higher-order content) is minimized
   wherever the mics are; keeping the pillow pair M1/M2 at the head wall
   parks that residual's minimum at your head as well, at no aesthetic
   cost since the bed head is already against a wall.
2. **≥ 1 m from every (present or future) woofer corner** — verified
   numerically: minimum over all pairs is 1.02 m (M4–S3).
3. **Off the tangential nodal lines.** A wall midline is a null of every
   odd mode along that wall — the resonant (1,1,0) included — so no mic
   sits near $x = L_x/2 = 2.22\ \mathrm{m}$ on the top/bottom walls or
   $y = L_y/2 = 1.83\ \mathrm{m}$ on the side walls (M3 keeps 0.38 m
   clearance, the others more).
4. **Height diversity straddling $H/2 = 1.35\ \mathrm{m}$** (elevation
   panel): four mics below, two above, so the second near-resonant mode
   (0,0,1) is observed with both signs.
5. **Non-degenerate geometry**: mics on three different walls at five
   heights — the $6 \times L$ matrix $\hat{S}$ stays well-conditioned for
   $L = 2$ now and $L = 4$ later.

**Why 6 and not 8 or 4.** The array must observe every significant mode at
every controlled tone with margin: ~2–3 modes at 59 Hz, ~3–4 in the
115–122 Hz cluster. Six over-determines that comfortably and tolerates one
disturbed mic (−17 % of the array). Four (the spec R5 minimum) still
handles the 59 Hz fundamental but leaves the harmonic-cluster observability
matrix $\Psi_{mn} = \psi_n(\mathbf{x}_m)$ square-ish — one bad position and
a mode goes nearly unobserved, the "quiet at the mics, loud between them"
failure. The [modal model](modes.qmd#observability-of-the-6-mic-array)
scores this layout's $\Psi$ conditioning numerically — full rank with
$\operatorname{cond}(\Psi) \le 6.6$ at every controlled tone; mic count
stands at six.

## Error microphones: mounting

The mics are Behringer ECM8000s — pencil-form **omnidirectional**
measurement condensers. The omni (pure-pressure) capsule simplifies
mounting twice over: there is no aim to control (a pressure reading is
orientation-free, unlike the cardioid alternative, whose pressure-gradient
component would make the reading direction-dependent), and pressure
capsules are intrinsically far less sensitive to body vibration than
gradient capsules. What remains:

- **Structure-borne pickup (residual).** The building vibrates at exactly
  the frequencies we care about, so cheap insurance is still worth it: pad
  each stock clip with foam (a suspension resonance
  $f_0 \approx 8\ \mathrm{Hz}$ attenuates 59 Hz body vibration by roughly
  $(f_0/f)^2 \approx -17\ \mathrm{dB}$), and prefer stands on rugs/pads
  over clamps on large resonant panels (a shaking headboard is the worst
  host). M5's dresser perch gets a foam pad under its stand.
- **Fixed position.** Orientation no longer matters, but position still
  becomes part of the identified $\hat{S}$: tape-mark each stand's
  footprint and re-run identification after any move or bump (R7).
- **Rental + cat.** Nothing fastens to walls — "at the wall" means a stand
  *beside* the wall. M1/M2 ride short boom arms clamped to the bed frame
  (through foam) or short weighted stands behind the headboard; M5 stands
  on the dresser (foam pad underneath); M3, M4 and M6 are weighted-base
  stands tight against their walls, where they're out of the walkable
  floor and hardest for the cat to reach. Leave no dangling cable slack
  (coil and tie at the stand base) and run the short baseboard cable runs
  through split-loom or cord covers — a batted-off mic is a
  re-identification event at best (R7) and a watchdog mute at worst (R8).

## Acceptance

The layout is validated, not assumed: after installation, run the
[verification plan](spec.qmd#measurement-and-verification-plan) — if the
measured attenuation at the grid points fails R2 while the error mics read
deep nulls, that is the near-field/observability signature, and the
response is to re-spread the mics (or trigger the 4-sub expansion), not to
raise loop gain.
